# Supervisor Agents and Multi-Agent Systems on Databricks {#supervisor-agents}

## Introduction

A single agent with a few tools can answer many questions. Real analytics
questions often cross domains, though: *"Why did conversions drop for the
spring campaign, and which audience should we test next?"* needs campaign
metrics, audience overlap, research reports, and perhaps a modeling job. A
**supervisor agent** handles this by coordinating specialized agents and tools.
It decides who should answer each part, delegates, and combines the results.

This chapter covers:

1. the supervisor pattern and when multiple agents help or hurt;
2. Databricks **Supervisor Agent**: how it works and how to build one;
3. what Databricks recommends for new work as of October 2026; and
4. a marketing-analytics example with descriptions, test questions, and
   evaluation.

It builds on MCP (Chapter \@ref(model-context-protocol)), context and harness
engineering (Chapter \@ref(context-harness-engineering)), and the analytics
tools in Chapter \@ref(classification-lookalike).

> **Status check (October 2026).** On 6 October 2026 the Databricks
> documentation labeled **Supervisor Agent a legacy offering**. For new low-code
> agents it recommends **Genie Agents**. To coordinate multiple agents in code
> it recommends the **Agent Bricks CLI**, which was in Beta at the time of
> writing. The related **Supervisor API** (Beta) was deprecated, with end of life
> on 30 September 2026. The *supervisor pattern* in this chapter remains
> current; the specific product is likely to change. Check the
> [Supervisor Agent page](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/agents/agent-bricks/multi-agent-supervisor)
> and [What is Agent Bricks?](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/agents/concepts)
> before building.

## The supervisor pattern

### What a supervisor does

A supervisor is an agent whose tools are *other agents* (and ordinary tools).
For each request it:

1. **interprets** the question and breaks it into parts;
2. **routes** each part to the subagent or tool whose description fits best;
3. **delegates** and collects the answers; and
4. **synthesizes** one response, or asks the user to clarify.

Anthropic describes the same idea as the *orchestrator–workers* workflow: a
central model breaks down a task, delegates subtasks to workers, and
synthesizes their results
([Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)).

### Common multi-agent shapes

| Pattern | How it works | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Router** | Sends the whole request to one specialist | Clearly separable domains (billing vs. analytics) |
| **Supervisor** | Splits the request, calls several specialists, combines results | Cross-domain questions |
| **Hierarchical** | A supervisor calls other supervisors | Large organizations with domain teams |
| **Pipeline** | Fixed sequence of steps | Repeatable workflows; often better as ordinary code |

### When multiple agents help, and when they hurt

**They help when:**

- domains have different data, permissions, and owners (each team curates its
  own Genie Agent);
- a specialist needs a focused context, which is the *isolate* technique from
  Chapter \@ref(context-harness-engineering); and
- subtasks can run independently and be combined.

**They hurt when:**

- the task needs one shared, detailed understanding that gets lost in
  handoffs;
- latency and cost matter, because every delegation adds model calls; and
- a fixed workflow would do. A scheduled job is simpler, cheaper, and easier to
  test than an agent deciding the steps each time.

A good rule: **start with one well-scoped agent, and add a supervisor only when
routing between distinct, well-defined specialists is the actual problem.**

## Databricks Supervisor Agent

The facts in this section come from the
[Supervisor Agent documentation](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/agents/agent-bricks/multi-agent-supervisor)
as of 6 October 2026.

### What it provides

Supervisor Agent builds a supervisor system that coordinates Genie Agents,
agent endpoints, Unity Catalog functions, MCP servers, and custom agents. It
produces a serving endpoint that you can query from AI Playground, the API, or
a Databricks App. Domain experts can improve its routing with
natural-language feedback. Databricks lists use cases such as market analysis
across research reports and usage data, internal-process questions, and
customer-service answers.

### Requirements

- Serverless compute and Unity Catalog enabled, in a supported region.
- Access to Model Serving and to a serverless usage policy with a nonzero
  budget.
- At least one subagent ready to use.
- End users need explicit access to each subagent (next table).

### Supported subagents and required end-user permissions

| Subagent or tool | Required end-user permission |
|---|---|
| Genie Agent | Access to the Genie Agent and its underlying Unity Catalog objects |
| Published dashboard | `CAN VIEW` on the dashboard |
| Knowledge Assistant endpoint | `CAN QUERY` on the endpoint |
| Model serving endpoint | `CAN QUERY` on the endpoint |
| Unity Catalog function | `EXECUTE` on the function |
| Unity Catalog table | `SELECT`, plus `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` |
| Unity Catalog volume | `READ VOLUME`, plus `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` |
| AI Search index (Delta Sync only) | `SELECT`, plus `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` |
| Another Supervisor Agent | `CAN QUERY` on it |
| Unity Catalog MCP Service | `EXECUTE`, plus `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` |
| Custom MCP server or custom agent on Databricks Apps | `CAN_USE` on the app |
| Web search (built in) | No extra permission; the user approves each search |

A supervisor can use **up to 50 agents and tools**.

**Access control is per user.** End users reach only the subagents and data
they are allowed to use. If a user can access none of the subagents, the
supervisor ends the conversation. If they can access only some, it steers away
from the others. This is the behavior an agency needs when different teams may
see different clients' data.

### Built-in code execution

Every supervisor includes a code execution tool. It runs model-generated
Python (default), SQL, or shell commands in a sandboxed serverless session with
**no internet access**. Its only data access is read-only access to the Unity
Catalog tables and volumes added as tools, subject to the end user's
permissions. Databricks warns that running arbitrary code can expose data the
agent can reach, so permissions and guardrails remain the customer's
responsibility.

### Web search

Web search uses the `databricks-gpt-5` Foundation Model API regardless of the
model that powers the supervisor. The workspace must allow that model, and web
search is unavailable in some regions and in workspaces with the Enhanced
Security and Compliance add-on. The supervisor asks the user to approve each
search before sending the query to the public web. Never let client data
appear in a web query.

### Building one: five steps

1. **Configure.** Go to **Agents → Create Agent → Supervisor Agent**. Add tools
   and subagents, and write a **description for each one**; the supervisor
   routes based on these descriptions. Optionally add supervisor-level
   **Instructions** and a user-facing **Description**.
2. **Test.** Chat in the right pane, or open the endpoint in AI Playground,
   where AI Judge and synthetic task generation may be available. Check that
   each question reaches the right subagent.
3. **Improve.** In the **Examples** tab, add representative questions. Share
   the configuration page with subject-matter experts (they need Can Manage on
   the agent and access to the subagents). Experts attach natural-language
   **Guidelines** to questions, and guidelines take effect when saved.
4. **Manage permissions.** Grant **Can Manage** (edit and improve) or **Can
   Query** (use the endpoint only) to users, groups, or service principals.
5. **Query the endpoint.** From AI Playground, **Get code** provides curl and
   Python examples for applications such as a Streamlit app on Databricks Apps.

### Managing supervisors with the SDK (Beta)

The Databricks SDK for Python can create supervisors and manage their tools.
From the documentation:

```python
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from databricks.sdk.service.supervisoragents import SupervisorAgent

w = WorkspaceClient()
supervisor_agent = SupervisorAgent(
    display_name="<display-name>",
    description="<description>",
    instructions="<instructions>",
)
created = w.supervisor_agents.create_supervisor_agent(supervisor_agent=supervisor_agent)
print(created)
```

Tools (subagents) are added with `w.supervisor_agents.create_tool(...)`, and
their descriptions can be updated with `update_tool`. This lets a team keep
supervisor configurations in version control and recreate them across
workspaces. See the documentation for the tool types and fields.

### Limitations

- At most 50 agents and tools per supervisor.
- AI Search subagents support only Delta Sync indexes.
- Web search has the regional and compliance restrictions above.
- It is a legacy offering, so plan for migration.

## What to use for new work (October 2026)

| Need | Databricks recommendation | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Low-code agent over tables and documents | **Genie Agents** | Curated with Unity Catalog metadata, example SQL, instructions, and trusted assets |
| Business users exploring data, dashboards, apps | **Genie One** | Can also be called as a tool by custom agents |
| Custom agent in code, including multi-agent coordination | **Agent Bricks CLI** (Beta) deploying to Agent Runtime | Scaffolds a project, runs locally, deploys with managed memory, sessions, tools, and MLflow tracing |
| Composing several agents, such as coding agents | **Omnigent** | Described by Databricks as a meta-harness |
| Existing Supervisor Agent | Keep running, plan migration | Legacy; no new investment |

Sources: [What is Agent Bricks?](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/agents/concepts),
[September 2026 release notes](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/release-notes/product/2026/september).

In code, the pattern stays the same. Databricks' multi-agent app template
builds an **orchestrator that treats each subagent as a tool**: Genie Agents
reached through their MCP server, other agents on Databricks Apps, and serving
endpoints. Each subagent has a name, an endpoint, and a detailed description
to improve routing
([multi-agent apps](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/agents/custom-agents/multi-agent-apps)).
That page uses the legacy agent server; follow the Agent Bricks CLI
documentation for new deployments.

**What carries over regardless of product:** clear subagent descriptions,
per-user permissions, a labeled set of test questions, and expert guidelines.
Building these now is not wasted if the product changes.

## Worked example: a campaign insights supervisor

An agency team wants one assistant for account leads that answers
cross-domain questions about a client's campaigns.

### The specialists

| Subagent or tool | Type | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| `campaign_performance` | Genie Agent over campaign metric views | Spend, impressions, reach, conversions, CPA by channel, market, and week |
| `audience_overlap` | Unity Catalog function | Size and overlap of two audience segments |
| `basket_affinity` | Unity Catalog function | Precomputed support, confidence, and lift for product pairs |
| `lookalike_jobs` | Custom MCP server on Databricks Apps | Start the validated lookalike job; check status and results |
| `research_library` | Document Q&A (Knowledge Assistant or AI Search index) | Client briefs, research reports, past campaign learnings |

### Write descriptions that route well

The supervisor routes on descriptions, so treat them as prompts. Compare:

> *Weak:* "Campaign data."

> *Strong:* "Answers quantitative questions about this client's paid-media
> campaigns: spend, impressions, reach, clicks, conversions, CPA, and ROAS by
> channel, market, campaign, and week, from 2024 onward. Use for 'how much',
> 'how did it change', and 'which channel' questions. Does not contain
> audience membership, product purchases, or research documents."

A strong description says **what the tool covers, when to use it, and what it
does not cover**. The "does not" part prevents many routing errors.

### Test questions and expected routing

| Question | Expected route |
|---|---|
| "What was CPA by channel last month in Germany?" | `campaign_performance` |
| "How much do our sports-fans and new-parents segments overlap?" | `audience_overlap` |
| "Which products are most often bought with running shoes?" | `basket_affinity` |
| "Why did spring conversions drop, and what did last year's brief say about seasonality?" | `campaign_performance` + `research_library` |
| "Build a 3% lookalike from the loyalty seed." | `lookalike_jobs`, after confirmation |
| "What's the weather in Paris?" | Politely decline (out of scope) |
| "Show me individual customer emails in the seed." | Decline (personal data) |

### Expert guidelines

Account leads and analysts add guidelines to example questions, such as:

- "When reporting CPA, always state the date range and currency."
- "Do not compare markets with different currencies without converting."
- "For lookalike requests, confirm the seed, size, and client before starting a
  job."
- "Overlap results come from the function; never estimate overlap from
  memory."
- "If a question mixes two clients, ask which client is meant."

### Agency-specific design choices

- **Client separation.** Use one supervisor per client, or Unity Catalog row
  filters and per-user permissions, so that no conversation can mix clients'
  data. Test this explicitly with users who lack access.
- **Numbers from tools.** Display numeric results from tool outputs, not from
  the model's prose. Apply the number-check sensor from Chapter
  \@ref(context-harness-engineering).
- **Actions need confirmation.** Starting a job costs money; require explicit
  user confirmation and log who approved it.
- **Web search off or tightly scoped.** Client names or results must not appear
  in public web queries.

## Evaluating a supervisor

Evaluate two things separately:

1. **Routing accuracy.** For each labeled question, did the supervisor call the
   expected subagents, and avoid the wrong ones? Trace data in MLflow shows
   which tools were called.
2. **Answer quality.** Are the numbers correct (they should match the tool
   output exactly), is the answer grounded, and did the supervisor clarify or
   decline when it should?

Practical steps:

- Build 30 to 50 labeled questions covering every subagent, multi-domain
  questions, out-of-scope requests, and permission edge cases.
- Run each question several times and report pass^k (all runs correct), not
  just one lucky run.
- Re-run the set after every change to descriptions, guidelines, or subagents.
  A better description for one tool can steal traffic from another.
- Use [MLflow GenAI evaluation](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor)
  with code-based checks for routing and number matching, and LLM judges or
  expert review for answer quality.

## Common pitfalls

| Pitfall | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Overlapping descriptions | Questions bounce between two subagents | Make scopes exclusive; add "does not cover" lines |
| Too many subagents | Slow, inconsistent routing | Merge narrow tools; add a supervisor only where domains truly differ |
| Missing user permissions | "I can't help with that" for some users | Grant access to each subagent, or explain the restriction |
| Synthesized numbers | The answer contains figures not in any tool output | Render numbers from tool outputs; add a number check |
| Silent actions | Jobs started without approval | Require confirmation for writing or spending actions |
| Untested changes | Quality drops after an edit | Re-run the labeled question set after every change |

## Exercise: design a supervisor on paper

1. List three to five specialists you already have or could build (a Genie
   Agent, two Unity Catalog functions, a document index).
2. Write a strong description for each, including what it does *not* cover.
3. Write 15 test questions with expected routes, including two multi-domain
   questions, two out-of-scope requests, and one permission edge case.
4. Write five expert guidelines.
5. Decide whether you need a supervisor at all, or whether one Genie Agent or a
   scheduled job would do.

## Key takeaways

- A supervisor routes, delegates, and synthesizes across specialists; it is the
  orchestrator–workers pattern.
- Use multiple agents only when distinct domains, permissions, or contexts
  justify them; otherwise one agent or a fixed workflow is simpler.
- Databricks Supervisor Agent coordinates up to 50 agents and tools, enforces
  per-user access, includes sandboxed code execution, and improves through
  expert guidelines.
- As of October 2026, Supervisor Agent is legacy. Use Genie Agents for low-code
  work and the Agent Bricks CLI for custom multi-agent code.
- Descriptions, permissions, labeled test questions, and guidelines are durable
  assets that survive product changes.
- Evaluate routing and answer quality separately, repeatedly, and after every
  change.
